title: What if…
lede: Three decisions where the story could have gone differently. The “What if” panels are speculation, labeled as such.

forks.actual: By Stolar’s account, EA’s Larry Probst asked for exclusive rights to sports games on the console. Stolar had just bought Visual Concepts for $10 million and refused: “Forget it then, end of story.”[^7] EA’s Bing Gordon was quoted saying “Dreamcast can’t succeed without EA.”[^7]
forks.whatif: With Madden and FIFA on the box, the machine would have had the best-known sports brands of the era, and one fewer reason to wait for a PlayStation 2. It would not have had NFL 2K, which, IGN wrote, many fans and critics preferred to Madden.[^20] Bellfield doubted any EA game would have changed the outcome.[^7]

forks.actual: The console used Sega’s own GD-ROM discs. Stolar says Sega could not afford a DVD drive, and a promised add-on never appeared.[^21] The PlayStation 2 played DVD movies.[^20]
forks.whatif: A DVD drive would have removed one of Sony’s clearest advantages and closed the CD-R piracy hole. It would also have raised the cost of a machine that Moore recalls was already sold below cost,[^9] and delayed a launch whose whole point was to arrive first.

forks.actual: In September 2000 Moore and Bellfield advised Tokyo to get out of hardware. The studio heads walked out of the meeting.[^7] The decision came on January 31, 2001, after the holiday season, with about 2 million consoles unsold.[^4]
forks.whatif: An exit announced before Christmas would have saved some of the ¥52.4 billion inventory write-off,[^2] but it would have killed holiday sales of the console and its games. Sega’s first year as a publisher produced an operating profit,[^3] which suggests the destination was right even if the timing was forced.
